documents.abstract: This study examines the role of gamification and serious games in Industry 4.0 and smart-factory environments. It explains how industrial production has developed from mechanization and mass production to interconnected, data-driven systems based on artificial intelligence, industrial control systems, digital twins, and the Industrial Internet of Things. Within this technological context, organizations face a growing need to train employees rapidly, maintain specialized competencies, and support continuous workplace learning. The study distinguishes between gamification, which introduces game elements into non-game practices, and serious games, which combine game structures with practical objectives such as training, decision-making, and skill development. It identifies three forms of workplace implementation: scheduled instructional games, idle time games, and learning while working. Their effectiveness depends on their integration with existing workflows, production data, cybersecurity requirements, and organizational objectives. One industrial case demonstrates the practical potential of game-based training. A digital-twin-based training system developed for Novo Nordisk enabled employees to practice complex production-planning decisions using realistic operational scenarios. The study further presents dystopian, utopian, and realistic future scenarios. These scenarios show that gamification may strengthen learning, cooperation, safety, and sustainability, but may also increase surveillance, competition, and performance pressure. The study concludes that industrial gamification should be transparent, adaptable, empirically evaluated, and subject to human oversight, workplace negotiation, and appropriate regulation.

As cybercrime costs are projected to reach $10.5 trillion annually by 2025 and the human factor accounts for 68% of data breaches, understanding variation in cybersecurity self-efficacy (CSE) across demographic groups has become a pressing research priority. Despite a growing body of CSE literature, systematic reviews have identified a near-complete absence of intergenerational comparative frameworks – a significant gap in both theory and practice. This study examines differences in CSE and cyber risk perception between Generation Z (born 1997–2012) and older adults (aged 60+), with gender, income, and digital financial service usage as boundary conditions. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey was conducted in Poland (January 2026) with 307 respondents. Validated Likert-scale instruments measured CSE, risk perception, and attitudes toward digital financial services; hypotheses were tested using Mann-Whitney U tests and Spearman’s rank correlation. Findings confirm that Generation Z exhibits significantly higher CSE than older adults, with the largest gaps concentrated in technically complex behaviors such as VPN use, multi-factor authentication configuration, and password manager utilization. Concurrently, older adults report substantially higher cyber risk perception despite lower self-efficacy, constituting a fear-capability asymmetry consistent with Protection Motivation Theory’s coping deficit mechanism. The income-CSE association was significant only within the older adult subsample. Gender differences in CSE were cohort-specific, with the standard male advantage reversing direction among older adults. These findings highlight the necessity of differentiated, generationally tailored cybersecurity education and policy interventions.

As human–AI interaction becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, users often infer social identities from AI systems, including gender. Moving beyond the conventional view of AI gender as a static, designer-assigned attribute, this study conceptualizes AI gender as a user-constructed perception shaped by contextual cues. Integrating social role theory, the stereotype content model, and ambivalent sexism theory, we conducted a 2 (AI gender cues: male vs. female) × 3 (interaction context: service-oriented, warm-authoritative, vs. serious-authoritative) between-subjects experiment with Chinese participants ( N = 833) to examine how interaction context, perceived AI gender, and sexist ideology jointly shape evaluations of AI competence, warmth, and trustworthiness. The results showed that interaction context significantly influenced gender attribution, with the serious-authoritative condition eliciting stronger gender categorization and a masculinization bias regardless of assigned gender cues. The evaluative consequences of perceived AI gender were also context-dependent: perceived femininity consistently linked with warmth, but was associated with competence and trustworthiness primarily in the serious-authoritative condition. Hostile and benevolent sexism further moderated these relationships in distinct ways. By shifting attention from designed gender to perceived gender, this study offers a more process-oriented account of AI anthropomorphism and demonstrates the value of integrating the stereotype content model with ambivalent sexism theory to explain bias in human–AI evaluation.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in corporate reporting, where accounting policies and estimates require professional judgment. This conceptual study examines how GenAI may assist preparers without displacing human responsibility or reinforcing managerial bias. Using theory adaptation, it integrates research on professional judgment, motivated reasoning and automation reliance. It identifies five bias-amplification mechanisms: anchoring, automation bias, outcome-directed prompting, unverified justification and diffusion of responsibility. The paper develops TRACE, a proposed framework comprising task boundary, regulatory grounding, alternative assessment, challenge and contradiction, and evidence trail. Its intended operation is illustrated through four constructed IFRS cases covering IAS 8 and IAS 16, IAS 36, IAS 37 and IFRS 15, three involving climate-transition assumptions. The AI proposals are stylised illustrations, not actual model outputs or empirical data. The analysis suggests that GenAI is most defensible when used to identify alternatives and contradictory evidence and to challenge a preferred treatment, and least defensible when asked to select or justify a conclusion. TRACE may make AI-assisted judgments more attributable and contestable, but it cannot guarantee unbiased or technically correct outcomes; independent human review remains necessary. The framework has not been empirically validated. It considers governance, control, reporting reliability and sustainable management.

documents.abstract: The hidden curriculum in nursing education refers to the implicit lessons transmitted through routines, relationships, and unit culture that shape how learners interpret what is truly valued in practice. Although it can strengthen professional identity and adaptive competence, it can also normalize unsafe shortcuts, silence, emotional detachment, and risk tolerance that undermine both safety-critical behaviors and compassionate care. This commentary reframes the hidden curriculum as a modifiable driver of patient safety and moral formation within clinical learning environments, using a human factors and systems lens to connect everyday signals to observable outcomes such as hand hygiene adherence, medication verification, handoff reliability, near-miss reporting, willingness to speak up, and respectful patient-centered interactions. A practical reform package is proposed that aligns educator role modeling, structured debriefing, psychologically safe team routines, and unit-level measurement with feasible evaluation within one academic year. Treating the hidden curriculum as part of work system design, rather than an unavoidable cultural residue, creates an actionable pathway for nursing programs and partner hospitals to improve safety while strengthening professional formation and mobility-ready practice norms. This commentary also situates the hidden curriculum within a Christian ethical framework, emphasizing compassion, dignity, truthfulness, humility, and service as core values that shape both patient safety and the formation of nurses as morally grounded professionals.

Influencer product advertisements and artificial intelligence (AI) generated content are increasingly present in social media. As companies evolve in their marketing strategies, the use of Virtual Influencers (VI) may be a lucrative way to connect with consumers on social media. Research on VI has found attractiveness, perceived trustworthiness, congruence, and credibility to have an impact on consumer purchasing intentions. However, little work has focused on directly comparing short-form human influencer advertisements to VI ones. In the present study, 64 participants viewed 8 short-form video advertisements, 4 with VI and 4 with human influencers, and answered survey questions about the influencers and products advertised. Results were mixed; across influencer and product statements, both VI and human influencer product advertisements were preferred uniquely. These findings show that VI may be a comparable option to human influencers for brands to promote their products on social media.

This study evaluated a 2-week robotics-based STEM camp as a human factors and ergonomics (HFE) intervention designed to enhance perceived engineering knowledge and motivation. Youth participants ( N ≈ 100, ages 9–17) engaged in robotics assembly, programming, and mechanical design activities using VEX EXP and K’NEX systems within competitive, sport-based challenges. Pre- and post-camp surveys assessed perceived engineering knowledge and motivation across multiple disciplines. Significant increases were observed across all perceived knowledge domains, including general, computer, mechanical, electrical, and industrial engineering. Significant motivational gains were observed for mechanical and industrial engineering. Findings support HFE principles linking structured practice, embodied interaction, feedback visibility, and competitive contextualization to competence development and engagement. Robotics-based STEM programs may represent scalable socio-technical interventions for promoting early engineering identity and motivation.

The transition to fifth- and sixth-generation fighter aircraft is increasing the psychophysiological demands placed on military aircrew. Next-generation fast-jet operations combine sustained and repetitive high-G loading; intermittent hypoxia, hyperoxia, and hypobaria associated with unexplained physiological episodes; prolonged single-seat missions; advanced helmet-mounted displays; acoustic and thermal stress; and high cognitive load from sensor fusion, automation, and manned-unmanned teaming. These exposures challenge autonomic regulation, cerebral and respiratory physiology, neurocognitive performance, sensory integration, and central nervous system resilience. This narrative review synthesizes evidence across cardiovascular-autonomic and hemodynamic function; respiratory physiology and unexplained physiological episodes in the on-board oxygen generating system era; cognitive workload, fatigue, and pilot experience; visual-oculomotor, vestibular, auditory, thermal, and musculoskeletal stress; biological markers of neural strain; and aircrew surveillance and countermeasures. The organizing construct is psychophysiological readiness: the integrated capacity to meet mission demands without disproportionate physiological cost or degraded decision quality. Evidence from direct fifth-generation studies, other fast-jet operations, simulators, and controlled aerospace analogues shows measurable changes in heart rate variability, cerebral oxygenation and perfusion, cortical activity, sensory function, and neurostructural biomarkers, but direct fifth-generation evidence remains limited and responses are strongly individualized and context dependent. Current surveillance remains largely episodic and domain-siloed. We therefore propose a staged monitoring framework combining validated cardiovascular-autonomic and hemodynamic measures with neurocognitive, sensory, wearable, and biomarker data, while treating AI/ML as an experimental analytic layer requiring prospective validation. Longitudinal, career-spanning monitoring could ultimately support earlier identification of vulnerability and evidence-based optimization of training, recovery, and countermeasures while preserving human aeromedical oversight.

documents.abstract: This study introduces a novel scoring system based on triangular fuzzy numbers (TFNs) and proposes a new scoring combination approach integrating the original rapid upper limb assessment (RULA) worksheet with a Bayesian Network (BN) model. The resulting method, named fuzzy Bayesian network-based RULA (FBnRULA), was evaluated by comparing it with the RULA method for assessing 14 different postures. The FBnRULA method showed a maximum difference of 1.75 and an average difference of 0.62 compared to RULA. This enhancement addresses the shortcomings of traditional methods that lack sensitivity to variations in input variables, which can hinder the accurate assessment of ergonomic interventions. The developed FBnRULA method demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting minimal changes in ergonomic postures following interventions in industrial settings.

Smartphones and social media platforms are integral to communication, education, employment, entertainment, and social interaction. Although research on problematic smartphone and social media use has focused mainly on psychological and behavioral outcomes, increasing evidence indicates relevant physical and musculoskeletal consequences. This narrative review synthesizes evidence concerning chronic musculoskeletal symptoms, postural and biomechanical factors, myofascial findings, and acute injuries associated with smartphone use, and considers behavioral injury pathways related to social media. Relevant systematic reviews, meta-analyses, observational studies, experimental investigations, emergency-department surveillance studies, and scholarly syntheses were identified through targeted literature searches and reference tracing. Intensive or problematic smartphone use is associated with symptoms involving the neck, upper back, shoulders, wrists, hands, and thumbs, although causal relationships remain uncertain. Acute-injury studies document sprains, strains, fractures, hand and wrist trauma, head and neck injuries, falls, and transportation-related injuries associated with mobile-device involvement. Pediatric studies and experimental pedestrian research support distraction as an important mechanism. Emerging evidence also documents physical harm associated with risky social-media challenges and social-media-related interpersonal violence. Smartphone- and social-media-related physical health risks therefore extend beyond chronic postural complaints and involve mechanical, attentional, environmental, and behavioral mechanisms. Prevention should combine ergonomic education, movement variability, distraction awareness, digital-health literacy, age-specific injury prevention, and responsible engagement with social-media content.

This article aims to examine the impacts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on contemporary legal practice. It begins with a historical overview of AI's emergence and its development to the present day, highlighting the technological advances that have reshaped the legal profession. Through a bibliographic review—especially based on the works of Cláudio Canuto and Thiago Massicano—the research analyzes the implementation of AI-based tools in law firms, their contributions to procedural efficiency, and the ethical and legal challenges they raise. In conclusion, the article projects the future of the legal profession, reflecting on the limits of replacing human performance with technological evolution.

Job satisfaction and organizational commitment are associated with employee performance, yet these relationships do not explain how favorable attitudes become effective contributions. This article develops a conceptual model of that transition through an integrative reading of research on work attitudes, meaningful work, social exchange, motivation, and work design. The model proposes that employees interpret satisfying work experiences in relation to organizational purposes, develop affective commitment, form intentions to reciprocate valued treatment, and direct available resources toward specific work activities. Organizational justice is proposed to condition selected attitudinal transitions, while the design of digital work may facilitate or obstruct the conversion of resource allocation into performance. The synthesis identifies three central problems in existing explanations: insufficient separation of adjacent constructs, limited evidence for temporal ordering, and the treatment of resources as available without examining their deployment. Eight propositions address these problems while retaining direct, reverse, and competing explanations. The article also specifies measurement boundaries, disconfirming observations, and a staged research agenda. Its contribution is a conditional account of how work attitudes may influence task, contextual, and other role contributions without treating commitment as sufficient for performance or additional effort as inherently beneficial. The model remains untested. Its value depends on whether the proposed mechanisms can be distinguished empirically and explain behavior beyond established constructs such as meaningful work, perceived support, and engagement.

Large language models have transformed the landscape of natural language processing, but their practical impact fades rapidly at the edges of under-resourced languages. Many linguistic communities lack the substantial digital footprint needed to effectively leverage standard foundation models. In this paper, we present a systematic review of recent adaptation literature to explore the strategies by which under-resourced languages can benefit from pretrained architectures, avoiding the need to train from zero. With a PRISMA-guided protocol, this study tracks multilingual backbones, localized LLMs, engineering practice, and evaluation metrics. The field’s trajectory is clear: research has largely moved away from generic multilingual representation learning towards language-specific fine-tuning, instruction alignment, parameter-efficient adaptations, vocabulary adaptation, and cross-lingual transfers. However, progress is uneven, with scarce data, poorly tuned benchmarks, and inconsistent access to computational resource challenging downstream usefulness. As demonstrated by our synthesis, architecture updates alone are insufficient; instead, technical adaptation and local resource cultivation must be seen as a single community-anchored ecosystem.

documents.abstract: Sikad drivers provide short-distance, pedal-powered transport in many Philippine communities, yet their working lives remain underrepresented in qualitative scholarship. This phenomenological study explored the lived experiences of ten long-term male sikad drivers in Ozamiz City, Misamis Occidental, Philippines. Participants were purposively selected from drivers who were married, had at least two children, and had more than 15 years of experience. In-depth interviews examined sources of motivation, everyday hardships, coping practices, and hopes for the future. The accounts were synthesised into four overarching themes: (1) family as the central source of purpose and dignity; (2) poverty, restricted opportunity, and social vulnerability; (3) faith and everyday coping; and (4) hope, perseverance, and resourcefulness. Participants described unstable earnings, difficulty meeting food and health needs, limited alternatives to informal work, road-safety concerns, competition from motorised transport, housing insecurity, and experiences of disrespect. At the same time, they emphasised responsibility to family, children's education, honesty, religious faith, gratitude, and persistent effort. The findings show that resilience among these drivers is relational and practical rather than simply individual: it is sustained by family obligations, spiritual meaning, everyday routines, and adaptive livelihood strategies while remaining constrained by informal employment and material insecurity. Because the sample was small, homogeneous, and context-specific, the findings are not intended to serve as population estimates. They nevertheless provide locally grounded evidence that can inform more inclusive discussions of informal transport, occupational health, road safety, social protection, and livelihood support.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in the social sciences as surrogates for human coders. Standard practice validates them by their correspondence with human measurements of the same stimuli using statistics like correlation. However, overall correspondence can conceal biases that distort specific claims. We demonstrate this with open-weight LLM ratings of 568 food and 1,811 scene photographs. Ratings inflate, attenuate, or reverse effects, and improving overall correspondence with prompts can improve one contrast while worsening another. Rankings also elevate some categories and demote others beyond what random errors of the same size typically produce. Across six prompts, some of these errors are shared, so sampling across prompts may continue to mask biases. We propose validating LLM coders against specific claims they will test rather than the general coding task.

Abstract This article examines how computational archival workflows transform fragile Holocaust last writings into machine-readable data, and what is lost in that transformation. It introduces the concept of material uncertainty: the condition of textual objects whose meaning cannot be separated from the damaged, improvised, or unstable material forms through which they survive. Drawing on Holocaust literary criticism, archival theory, material trauma studies, and debates over computation in cultural heritage, the article reconstructs a typical archival workflow, from image preprocessing, segmentation, and text recognition to post-processing, translation, metadata generation, and classification. It then executes this workflow on three Holocaust last-writing limit cases: Eva Schulzová’s illustrated poem “One Night in Terezín,” Eliezer Heiman’s inscribed clay tablets, and Sal Bramson’s cloth fragment. The workflow traces show that computational tools can enhance visibility, recover words, support translation, and create access, but also risk detaching textual content from the material conditions that make these objects evidentiary. Schulzová’s poem is reorganized as recoverable verbal text while its relation among image, line, and child authorship is flattened; Heiman’s clay resists extraction because depth, soot, and flaking occupy the same visual field; Bramson’s cloth shows how partial computational success may obscure relations among drawing, caption, textile, address, and clandestine transmission. The article argues that responsible workflows must be relation-preserving rather than extraction-driven, keeping uncertainty visible rather than resolving it into cleaner data.

Mental health misconceptions are widespread, yet it remains unclear how accurately psychology students distinguish such misconceptions from evidence-based information, whether this differs across stages of psychology education, and how their performance compares with that of large language models (LLMs). We evaluated the accuracy of 150 psychology students, including 70 first-semester and 80 more advanced students, in classifying 15 mental health myths and 15 facts. Additionally, we used Chat GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek V3.2, and GLM-5 to classify the same statements across 80 independent runs per statement and model. Students classified mental health myths more accurately than facts, and advanced students outperformed first-semester students in classifying both statement types (myths: 87.7% vs. 75.2%; facts: 69.3% vs. 55.4%). A binomial generalized linear mixed-effects model indicated that group differences in classification accuracy varied between myths and facts. LLMs generally showed higher accuracy than both student groups in classifying statements, although performance varied substantially across models, particularly for facts. Item-level analyses revealed partly distinct error patterns: students and LLMs struggled with some of the same facts, whereas they also showed relative advantages on specific statements. These findings suggest that mental health literacy differs significantly across stages of psychology education and that, although current LLMs perform strongly on this classification task, some item-specific errors recurred across repeated runs. Examining which misconceptions and facts remain difficult may help identify specific gaps in both psychology education and AI-generated mental health information.

Accurately predicting human performance during prolonged wakefulness is essential for safety in high-risk environments, where operators are often required to maintain wakefulness over extended periods without sleep. The present study integrates the circadian process (Process C) and the sleep homeostatic process (Process S) into the Queuing Network-Model Human Processor-Unified (QN-MHP-U) via Server 9 to predict human performance during prolonged wakefulness. The model is applied to a system monitoring task, where operators must monitor analog gauges and warning lights and respond promptly to abnormal signals—a task type that is both representative of real-world monitoring duties and highly vulnerable to arousal decline. The model predicts reaction time on this task over 25 hr of wakefulness, achieving an RMSE of 0.41. The developed computational model can be further applied to domains requiring long-duration work, such as aviation and nuclear power operations.

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Bronchoscopy is physically demanding, and studies of ergonomics and objective skill assessment require accurate, segment-resolved capture of the bronchoscopist's hand and head movements. However, existing motion capture approaches typically rely on specialized laboratory infrastructure or wearable sensor arrays, limiting their routine use. METHODS: A board-certified pulmonologist performed 10 systematic bronchoscopies across the 18 named segments using an airway simulator and a single-use bronchoscope. Procedures alternated between conditions without and with engagement of the bronchoscope's insertion-tube rotation mechanism. A custom visionOS application running on Apple Vision Pro captured bilateral hand and head poses at 30 Hz, with synchronized voice-cue annotations for each segment. RESULTS: All 180 expected segment insertions were recorded (94.4% via voice cues; 5.6% recovered through tracking-derived hold detection and excluded from per-insertion analyses). Intermittent tracking-freezing artifacts, in which a static pose was retained under a valid tracking flag, were detected by frame-to-frame immobility and excluded from the affected analyses. The mean per-insertion peak left-wrist rotation across all segments was 107.9° without and 72.6° with the rotation mechanism. The mean left-thumb path length within the wrist's local reference frame was 3.82 ± 0.48 m per bronchoscopy, and the estimated number of bronchoscope lever operation cycles was 64.8 ± 7.9 per procedure. CONCLUSION: In this proof-of-concept study, a single off-the-shelf head-mounted device enabled multi-channel capture of bronchoscopist kinematics during simulated bronchoscopy. This approach provides a practical methodological foundation for future studies on bronchoscopy ergonomics, skill assessment, and AI-driven training data generation.

Natural and technological disasters pose significant threats to public health, and their frequency and severity are intensifying under the influence of climate change. This chapter examines the full spectrum of disaster types, including hurricanes, floods, tsunamis, droughts, and technological events such as oil spills and train derailments, and explores their public health consequences across mortality, mental health, communicable disease, maternal and child health, occupational health, and environmental health services. The disaster management cycle, encompassing preparedness, response, mitigation, and recovery, is presented as a policy framework, with attention to the governance architecture that guides action at federal, state, and local levels. Key legislation, including the Stafford Act, PAHPA, and major environmental statutes, is reviewed alongside case studies of Hurricane Katrina, the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, and repeated disaster events to illustrate real-world policy successes and failures. The chapter highlights community resilience as both a policy goal and a measurable capacity and addresses emerging challenges, including aging infrastructure and data-sharing barriers. Practical tools for public health decision-makers and opportunities offered by AI-enhanced surveillance and remote sensing are also discussed.

Abstract Across East Asia, emotional AI in healthcare is governed through markedly different normative and institutional rationalities that construct the patient, harm, and vulnerability in distinct ways. This article develops a triadic analytical framework, integrating moral anthropologies, models of legitimacy, and regulatory instruments, to examine governance rationalities in Japan, China, and Hong Kong. Instead of treating Asian perspectives as variations on Euro-American principlism, this analysis examines these jurisdictions in their own right, showing how each constructs the patient differently, as relational node, protected subject, or rights-holder, and prioritises different harms accordingly. Using PARO, a therapeutic companion robot deployed globally in elderly care, as a stylised analytical device, the article shows that the same robot becomes three different regulatory objects. This case study surfaces a fourth dimension of governance rationality: temporal orientation. Japan’s governance rationality is iterative, allowing norms to emerge through use and professional dialogue; China’s is preventive, anticipating and regulating harms before deployment; and Hong Kong’s is reactive, adjudicating violations after they occur. These temporal orientations shape harm-prevention outcomes as consequentially as the choice of instruments, and constitute the article’s primary empirical contribution. Extending Cheong’s analysis of structural accountability gaps and Zuboff’s account of how institutional power determines which technological harms become actionable, the comparison suggests that vulnerability, harm, and accountability function as governance-produced categories rather than as properties inherent to the technology. The article argues that governing emotional AI requires not harmonisation of principles but recognition of ontological difference, an epistemological reorientation with direct implications for transnational governance frameworks.

Axial Spondyloarthritis (axial SpA) is often missed in young people, often confused with mechanical Low Back Pain (LBP), especially among those with heavy manual labour, resulting in poor management and loss of function. This case report details a 22-year-old male farm labourer who had suffered from chronic LBP (4/10 with activity and 7/10 at rest) for 1.5 years, progressive stiffness in the spine (morning stiffness> 60 minutes), and decreased work capacity. On clinical examination, decreased lumbar mobility (flexion 40°), decreased chest expansion (2.5 cm), posterior chain muscle tightness, and guarded movement without neurological deficit were noted. Laboratory investigations revealed an elevated ESR (42 mm/hour), a borderline normal C-Reactive Protein (CRP: 4.2 mg/L; reference <5 mg/L), which, while within the normal range, may carry diagnostic relevance in axial SpA, and negative HLA-B27 and rheumatoid factor. Unilateral grade II sacroiliitis (modified NY criteria) and vertebral squaring with early syndesmophytes were seen on radiographs, compatible with seronegative radiographic axial SpA. The patient fulfilled the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis International Society (ASAS) criteria for radiographic axial SpA (sacroiliitis on imaging plus ≥1 SpA feature). Amor classification criteria confirmed the diagnosis at the minimum threshold (score 6, threshold ≥6); notably, the radiological sacroiliitis item scored 0 points as unilateral grade II sacroiliitis does not meet the Amor radiological criterion (which requires bilateral ≥ Grade II or unilateral ≥ Grade III), and the total of 6 points was reached through clinical features alone. Baseline assessment indicated high disease activity and functional limitation {Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) 5.6; Functional Index (BASFI): 5.3; Metrology Index (BASMI): 2.4; Global Score (BAS-G): 8.5}. A structured 12-week physiotherapy program including spinal mobility and extension exercises, flexibility training, breathing exercises and postural correction was implemented, along with occupationspecific ergonomic interventions including neutral spine lifting, load redistribution (≤15 kg), work modification, and use of longhandled tools. At 12-week follow-up, clinically meaningful improvements were observed: BASDAI score was 3.4, BASFI score was 3.1, BASMI score was 1.6, BAS-G score was 4.2, pain score 3/10 during activity and 5/10 at rest, and a 34% improvement in work productivity (Work Productivity and Activity Impairment (WPAI) questionnaire). Improvements in BASDAI and BASFI exceeded established Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) thresholds. This case emphasises early recognition of inflammatory back pain. It highlights the role of physiotherapy combined with occupation-specific ergonomic modifications in improving function and work participation among manual workers with seronegative axial SpA.

Background/Objectives: Occupational Contact Dermatitis (OCD) is one of the most common occupational diseases and represents a substantial clinical and socioeconomic burden. Despite its high prevalence, OCD is frequently underrecognised and underreported, limiting the effectiveness of occupational health surveillance and preventive strategies. This study aimed to investigate the extent of OCD underreporting in Italy by comparing official reporting data with incidence estimates derived from epidemiological data available in the scientific literature. Methods: Official data on dermatitis and eczema cases reported to the Italian National Institute for Insurance against Accidents at Work (INAIL) between 2020 and 2024 were analysed and compared with incidence estimates obtained through a systematic literature search of epidemiological studies, surveillance systems, and cohort studies conducted in high-risk occupational groups with available specific incidence data in the scientific literature, such as healthcare workers, construction workers, and hairdressers. Results: INAIL data showed an average of approximately 182 reported OCD cases per year during the study period. However, the estimates we calculated suggested a substantially higher disease burden, with an annual estimate ranging from 1439 cases to 21,412 cases. This implies that, depending on the incidence source used, only 0.8% to 12.7% of the expected cases are notified. Conclusions: OCD appears to be substantially underreported in Italy. Underrecognition of its occupational origin, the low severity often attributed to symptoms, and the limits of current surveillance systems likely contribute. Better occupational health surveillance, greater awareness among clinicians and workers, and simpler reporting procedures would improve case recognition and help prevent progression to chronic disease.

Objectives To investigate the differences in chronic disease prevalence and underlying metabolic profiles among working-age individuals across six typical occupational groups, identify occupation-related associated factors, and provide epidemiological evidence for occupation-specific precise prevention and control of chronic diseases. Methods A cross-sectional study design was adopted. A total of 1,473 on-the-job physical examinees aged 18–64 who received physical examination at the Physical Examination Center of the First Hospital of Lanzhou University from August 2024 to August 2025 were retrospectively included. Structured questionnaires were distributed via targeted online channels to collect sociodemographic characteristics and behavioral and lifestyle data. Physical examinations and laboratory tests were performed to obtain 16 health indicators. Age-standardized prevalence (ASR) of five chronic diseases (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and obesity) was calculated using the direct standardization method, with the age composition of the full study sample as the standard population. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was conducted to assess the independent associations between various factors and chronic diseases, and Spearman rank correlation analysis was used to evaluate the strength of associations between health indicators. Results Occupational disparities in the prevalence of hyperlipidemia and hyperuricemia were the most prominent. After age standardization, the prevalence of hyperlipidemia in police officers (ASR = 0.435, 95% CI 0.368–0.502) and software engineers (ASR = 0.418, 95% CI 0.366–0.470), as well as the prevalence of hyperuricemia in firefighters (ASR = 0.381, 95% CI 0.315–0.447) and police officers (ASR = 0.332, 95% CI 0.267–0.396) were all significantly higher than those in healthcare workers (ASR = 0.218 for hyperlipidemia and 0.143 for hyperuricemia, respectively), with no overlap in 95% CIs across occupational groups. Multivariate logistic regression analysis showed that police officers (OR = 2.499, 95% CI 1.409–4.433) and software engineers (OR = 2.531, 95% CI 1.007–6.361) were independent associated factors for hyperlipidemia; police officers (OR = 3.425, 95% CI 1.821–6.441), firefighters (OR = 4.143, 95% CI 1.916–8.955), and software engineers (OR = 2.957, 95% CI 1.136–7.696) were independent associated factors for hyperuricemia. No statistically significant occupational disparities were observed for hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and obesity. Correlation analysis showed that triglyceride, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, body mass index, uric acid and alanine aminotransferase formed a moderate correlation cluster (| r | = 0.44–0.54), body mass index was widely correlated with a variety of metabolic indicators ( r = 0.39–0.51), and uric acid was strongly correlated with creatinine ( r = 0.64). Conclusion Police officers, firefighters, and software engineers are occupational groups with elevated prevalence of hyperlipidemia and hyperuricemia. Age standardization is a necessary methodological step for cross-occupational health comparisons. Obesity occupies a core hub position in the metabolic comorbidity network. These findings provide reference evidence for developing occupation-specific, tiered precise prevention and control strategies for chronic diseases.

The number of migrant workers for temporary labor has rapidly increased, alongside high mortality rates in South Korea. This study explores the occupational safety and health conditions of migrant workers employed under the Employment Permit System (EPS). Data were collected through in-depth interviews with 11 EPS migrant workers who had experienced occupational injuries and illnesses, supplemented by secondary data such as official government guidelines, administrative manuals, and relevant legislation. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The results are as follows: first, regarding migrant workers' perceptions of the workplace environments that contributed to occupational injuries and illnesses, four subthemes were identified: restricted access to EPS workplace information; assignment to small-scale workplaces; inadequate safety training; and nominally conducted safety inspections. Second, three subthemes emerged regarding the contexts that prevented migrant workers from appropriately responding to their occupational injuries and illnesses: inaccessibility of medical services; institutional barriers to the Workers' Compensation System; and lack of the right to transfer workplaces. Based on the results, this study highlights the importance of linking occupational health and safety policy with labor migration policy.

The metabolic cost of walking is widely used to evaluate human performance and effectiveness of clinical interventions. Decades of laboratory research, largely based on treadmill experiments, have established a canonical relationship between walking speed and metabolic cost, and suggested that ageing shifts this relationship upward, implying reduced efficiency in older adults. However, this relationship has not been well tested during overground walking across matched speeds. We compared healthy younger (n=16; 26±2yr) and older (n=11; 74±3yr) adults across eight outdoor overground walking trials at different speeds: preferred walking speed (PWS), three fixed speeds (0.8, 1.2, 1.6 m·s⁻¹), and four speeds at ±5% and ±10% of PWS. Contrary to our hypothesis, older adults did not show higher gross or net metabolic cost of walking (GCOW and NCOW) than younger adults at any speed; rather, both trended consistently lower in older adults, reaching significance for GCOW at 0.8 m·s⁻¹ only. Comparisons of resting metabolic rate and respiratory exchange ratio to prior reference groups did not indicate that our older cohort was unusually fit. Independent of age, GCOW was significantly higher at 0.8 m·s⁻¹ than at the remaining speeds (1.2-1.6 m·s⁻¹), confirming that walking at slower speeds increases GCOW. These findings challenge the view that ageing intrinsically increases the energetic cost of walking, suggesting instead that previously reported upward shifts in cost may reflect treadmill-specific constraints or speed effects. Future work is needed to explore direct comparisons of outdoor, overground walking with treadmill walking at fixed speeds in both younger and older adults.

One Health is an integrative framework that recognizes the functional interdependence of human, animal, plant, and ecosystem health. This chapter examines the concept&s;s historical evolution; its policy landscape at the city, state, national, and international levels; and the ongoing gaps that limit effective implementation. Beginning with foundational definitions and the drivers of One Health relevance, including zoonotic disease emergence, climate change, land-use change, antimicrobial resistance, and biodiversity loss, the chapter surveys U.S. policies across human health, animal health, plant health, and ecosystem protection. Case studies on H5N1 in dairy cattle and poultry and COVID-19 wastewater surveillance illustrate both progress and shortcomings in cross-sector coordination. Occupational health risks at the human–animal interface are also addressed. Key policy gaps identified include siloed data systems, uneven investment in One Health workforce development, lagging environmental surveillance, and disparities between high-income countries and low- and middle-income countries. The chapter concludes by highlighting emerging opportunities, including regional consortia and national academy initiatives, to accelerate intersectoral collaboration and build a more resilient One Health policy framework.

Decision makers are often called on to choose a single item from a menu of options: employees pick health plans from provider-sponsored lists, citizens vote for a representative among candidates, physicians select a treatment from an order set. Because options are often organized or grouped into subsets, the question arises whether the grouping of menu items affects the options ultimately selected by decision makers. Across ten experiments, we provide robust evidence of single-item partition dependence — decision makers are more likely to choose from response categories that are more finely partitioned, holding the underlying set of options constant. For example, an employee choosing a health plan from a menu that lists HMOs individually but groups PPOs into a single category with sub-options may be biased toward choosing an HMO. Unlike prior work on multi-item allocation decisions, the traditional explanation of partition dependence — a bias toward even allocation — cannot apply to single-item choice, because singular choices are not divisible. Instead, we find that finer partitions receive greater choice share because decision makers infer that separately listed options are more popular on average than grouped ones. More broadly, strategic partitioning of the menu space may serve as a simple and effective tool for managers, policymakers, and choice architects: listing options separately rather than grouping them together tends to increase their choice share, without fundamentally altering the underlying set of alternatives or the effort required to choose among them.

Abstract European classrooms have become increasingly diverse, raising questions for schools about how to support newly arrived migrant (NAM) pupils as they navigate academic and social transitions. This paper is an explorative, qualitative study of peer mentoring programmes for NAM pupils in the Netherlands, Spain, and Ireland and presents a comparison of the countries’ mentoring program systems. It focuses on recognition, design, and perceived outcomes of these programmes. Despite the small number of surveyed teachers ( n = 47) and pupils ( n = 43) and an uneven distribution of teachers between the countries, a conclusion can be that peer mentoring is not widely recognised or implemented, partly due to a narrow conceptualization or misrecognition of peer mentoring. Among schools that implement mentoring, programmes vary in design but share a focus on social connection and academic support. They mostly rely on voluntary participation and intrinsic motivation and have little structure, training, compensation, and feedback. Teachers generally report positive perceived outcomes, while pupil responses showed strong individual variation. No consistent differences emerged between countries or education systems.

Conventional Pancasila and Citizenship Education often remains teacher-centered, potentially contributing to cognitive fatigue and academic anxiety while limiting students’ meaningful engagement with learning. This study examines the implementation of the Deep Learning approach through three interconnected pillars—Mindful, Meaningful, and Joyful Learning—and explores its influence on students’ learning behaviors and psychological responses. Using a descriptive qualitative design, the study involved one fifth-grade teacher and nine fifth-grade students at State Elementary School 060814 Medan as key informants. Data were collected across four classroom meetings through participatory observation using teacher-behavior and student-learning-behavior indicators, complemented by in-depth interviews. The findings revealed a consistent improvement in the teacher’s implementation of the three pillars, including more effective reflective activities through Sharing Circles. Students demonstrated a shift from surface-level memorization toward deeper information processing and contextual understanding. Interview findings further indicated reduced academic anxiety, increased confidence and self-efficacy, and stronger intrinsic motivation. These findings suggest that Deep Learning can foster a more reflective, meaningful, and psychologically supportive environment for Pancasila and Citizenship Education.

BACKGROUND: Military aviation in distant operations increases aircrew fatigue and the risk of human-factor-related safety incidents. This study evaluated the impact of different fatigue management and pharmacological human augmentation approaches on flight safety and, in a separate analysis, the effect of prior spatial disorientation (SD) simulator training on in-flight SD severity. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed human-factor-related safety incidents in the Israeli Air Force across three operational periods: Operation 'Iron Swords' (short-range, lower-tempo), 'Rising Lion' (12-day long-range, high-tempo) and 'Epic Fury' (42-day extended-duration, high-tempo). The primary outcome was the normalised rate of safety incidents per flight hour. Secondary outcomes included the normalised utilisation of caffeine and modafinil and the severity of SD events among trained versus untrained aircrew. RESULTS: Across the three periods, 949 incidents were reported. Normalised incident rates and severity distributions remained stable between 'Rising Lion' and 'Epic Fury', despite the latter's significantly greater flight volume. The fighter fleet, the only platform to fully implement preplanned, individualised flight-and-rest scheduling and personalised stimulant prescriptions, was also the only platform to demonstrate a decrease in normalised incident rates (r=-0.82, p=0.004). Aircrew who had never undergone SD simulator training sustained significantly more severe SD events than previously trained aircrew (p=0.015). CONCLUSIONS: Implementing individualised physiological envelopes-combining personalised pharmacological augmentation with structured rest-was associated with stable or reduced in-flight safety incident rates during sustained, high-tempo operations. Additionally, prior SD simulator training was associated with a decreased level of severity of SD events.

Abstract Play is fundamental to children’s daily activities and provides a critical avenue for learning and development. However, attempts to describe and operationalize play are dominated by adults’ perspectives. This study aims to explore the subjective meaning of play to young children. Using a qualitative approach, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 327 children aged 4 to 8 years from [a Western European country]. These interviews were analyzed using both deductive and inductive content analysis methods to categorize children’s descriptions of play. Approximately half of the children provided coherent, differentiated descriptions of play. Results indicate that children’s perceptions align deductively with the features of play seminally defined by Krasnor and Pepler (1980) and expanded by Smith and Vollstedt (1985): positive affect, flexibility, intrinsic motivation, nonliterality, and means before end. The inductive analysis identified three additional categories, children’s business, social interactions, and object reference and therefore revealed additional features of play relevant for children. This study underscores the importance of recognizing children’s voices in research and highlights the complex, multifaceted nature of play from a child’s perspective. These insights into children’s perspectives contribute to a deeper understanding of play and inform educators, parents, and policymakers about the elements to play in early childhood. Future research should continue to explore the nuanced views of children to better support their developmental needs through play.

documents.abstract: This study examines entrepreneurs’ awareness and preventive activities regarding the environment and employees as key elements of the Quality 5.0 concept. Quantitative research was conducted among 380 manufacturing companies in Greater Poland that had not implemented or certified a quality management system. Data were collected using CATI interviews using an original questionnaire assessing the importance and implementation of 24 preventive management factors, with a detailed analysis of 10 factors. The findings identify maintaining good relations with the environment (K2), careful supplier selection and continuous evaluation (K3), improving employee qualifications and skills (K7), and ensuring occupational safety and ergonomics (K8) as the most important preventive management factors. The combined IPA and paired analyses identify K7—improving employee qualifications and skills—as the clearest improvement priority: it was the only factor in the “concentrate here” quadrant, had the largest importance–implementation gap (0.34), and the largest rank-biserial effect (rrb = 0.639). K2—maintaining good relations with the environment—and K8—ensuring occupational safety and ergonomics—combined high importance with high implementation and should therefore be maintained, while K5—selection of employees based on their competencies—also warrants attention due to its gap of 0.28. Paired Wilcoxon tests showed statistically significant implementation shortfalls for all ten factors after Holm correction, indicating that the gap between perceived importance and implementation is systematic. Participatory management (K6) received the lowest importance and implementation ratings, although its large paired effect suggests that its relatively low IPA priority should not be interpreted as evidence of low relevance. Associations with company size and years in operation were generally weak and factor-specific. The results contribute to understanding preventive management as a basis for sustainable, human-centered, and proactive Quality 5.0 practices. They suggest that managerial priorities should consider both the relative IPA position and the magnitude of importance–implementation gaps, with particular attention to employee competence development and participatory management. The results emphasize the role of preventive management practices in supporting the Quality 5.0 concept and provide practical guidance for organizations seeking to strengthen sustainable, employee-oriented, and proactive management approaches.

The changing nature of the modern workplace requires that employees take greater responsibility for managing their own careers. With the hospitality sector being the industries with high turnover, understanding the factors that influence employee retention has become important. This paper aims to provide a conceptual framework for examining the relationship between protean career orientation and the intention to quit, with flow proposed as a psychological mediator. This study integrates Protean Career Theory and Flow Theory, proposing that flow mediates how self-driven and values-driven protean career orientations influence the intention to quit. Protean individuals are suggested to be less likely to leave their organizations because their intrinsic motivation, deep absorption, and meaningful work engagement lead them to experience flow. This study provides theoretical, empirical, conceptual and practical contributions through the proposed framework. The findings suggest that employee motivation and retention can be sustained through creating work environments that foster autonomy and personal growth.

Dark rides are popular, archetypal theme park attractions, yet empirical research on their visitor experience remains limited. This study provides a quantitative exploration of Cornelis and Strijbosch's (2024) dark ride experience model, which describes how immersion, emotions, cognitions, and attentional switching (driven by switch factors of motivation, opportunity and ability) shape overall evaluations. Using self-report data from 770 visitors across nine dark rides at a Western European theme park, collected with a purpose-built post-experience survey, we tested 15 derived hypotheses. Results offer partial, context-bound support: switch factors, immersion, and positive emotions consistently predicted overall evaluations both directly and indirectly, whereas findings on cognitive engagement and negative emotions remain inconclusive. Implications for future dark ride research, design and development are discussed.

This study aims to analyze the application of Activity-Based Costing (ABC) in determining the cost of production (HPP) for food-processing MSMEs in Bekasi City. MSMEs play an important role in Indonesia’s economy but still face challenges in achieving accurate HPP due to conventional costing methods that often produce cost distortions. ABC is chosen because it allocates costs based on actual activities consuming resources, thus providing more accurate and relevant cost information. This research employs a contextual qualitative approach by exploring the experiences of MSME actors in implementing ABC, including human factors, work culture, and resource limitations. The focus is not only on HPP accuracy but also on the impact of ABC on cost efficiency and pricing strategies. The findings are expected to show that ABC enhances MSME competitiveness through more realistic cost calculations, control of non-value-added activities, and competitive pricing. The novelty of this study lies in developing a conceptual ABC model relevant to Indonesian MSMEs, as well as integrating simple digital accounting technology to support sustainable implementation. Therefore, this research contributes to strengthening MSME cost systems and provides a basis for policies and managerial accounting training in the small business sector.

Background. The article examines the current problem of rapid updating of topographic plans at a scale of 1 : 500 in conditions of an urgent need for rapid updating of geospatial data for the needs of engineering and cadastre. The use of traditional methods of ground surveying often turns out to be ineffective due to high labor intensity. The integration of modern unmanned systems into the workflow ensures the generation of detailed orthophoto maps with ultra-high resolution. The purpose of the study is to substantiate and develop practical recommendations for the use of modern topographic field aerial survey complexes for updating large-scale terrain plans. Methods. Modern topographic complexes DJI Inspire 2 and specialized P316 systems were used to conduct the study. The research methodology is based on a complex combination of advanced photogrammetric processing of image data in the Pix4Dmatic environment and subsequent vectorization of objects in ArcGIS Pro. Special attention is paid to the use of high-precision positioning technologies Real Time Kinematic and Post-Processed Kinematic for determining coordinates of the ground control points (GCPs). This approach makes it possible to ensure strict adherence to geometric parameters when building digital terrain models and to automate the process of creating a topographic database. Results. During the study, optimal technical parameters of aerial photography and digital data processing algorithms were established, allowing to stably achieve the root mean square error of the position of objects within 0.05 m. The study demonstrates the significant advantages of modern specialized software in substantially increasing the overall productivity of surveying professionals. It is experimentally proven that the use of the Pix4Dmatic and ArcGIS Pro combination allows to significantly reduce the time for office-based processing, while ensuring a high level of detail and accuracy required for 1 : 500 scale plans. Conclusions. A comprehensive technological scheme for updating plans has been proposed and tested, which ensures high accuracy of the results obtained and significantly reduces the time for performing office work due to a high degree of automation of the main processes. The implementation of the methodology based on modern topographic field aerial survey systems allows minimizing the impact of the human factor and optimizing resource requirements when creating large-scale cartographic products. The practical application of the developed recommendations confirmed their effectiveness for operational territory monitoring, which is critically important for updating geospatial databases in modern conditions.

The increase in occupational accidents and ergonomic risks in intralogistics operations represents a recurring problem in warehouses, especially during loading, unloading, and material handling activities, where traditional layout and optimization tools are insufficient to simultaneously integrate operational and human criteria. In response to this issue, this study developed and validated an integrated warehouse design framework aimed at reducing ergonomic risks and improving operational performance. The proposed approach combines the Supplier-to-Warehouse model, ABC inventory analysis, and a user-centered hybrid Variable Neighborhood Search–Genetic Algorithm (VNS-GA). A mixed-methods, quasi-experimental approach was applied in two SMEs located in Hidalgo, Mexico. Results showed significant improvements in operational times, travel distances, productivity, incident reduction, and ergonomic risk, demonstrating that integrating ergonomic and operational criteria enhances efficiency, safety, and worker well-being. En respuesta a esta problemática, este estudio desarrolló y validó un marco integrado de diseño de almacenes orientado a reducir los riesgos ergonómicos y mejorar el desempeño operativo. Se aplicó un enfoque de métodos mixtos con diseño cuasiexperimental en dos pequeñas y medianas empresas (PYMES) ubicadas en Hidalgo, México. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of smart health and elderly care to evaluate its research status, trends, and future directions. We analysed 4,828 articles from Web of Science and 109 from CNKI published from 2015 to 2025 using CiteSpace and VOSviewer. The analysis covers publication trends, co-authorship, institutional and author distribution, journal sources, co-cited literature, keyword co-occurrence and clustering, and emerging terms. WOS literature focuses on technology applications, interventions and ethical reflections, while CNKI literature emphasises policy and industry perspectives. Shared interests include humanistic concerns and digital equity. Future research should advance theory, methodology, and development pathways. This review provides insights for interdisciplinary collaboration and the sustainable development of smart health and elderly care.

documents.abstract: This registration documents the protocol as executed for a systematic review examining how responsible and ethical artificial intelligence can function as a strategic organisational capability and contribute to competitive advantage in the finance and healthcare sectors. The review addresses four research questions: (1) Which responsible-AI dimensions dominate research in finance and healthcare? (2) Through what mechanisms can responsible AI contribute to competitive advantage? (3) How do these mechanisms differ between finance and healthcare? and (4) Which organisational and environmental conditions determine whether responsible AI becomes a strategic capability rather than a compliance cost? The review covers responsible-AI dimensions including fairness, transparency and explainability, accountability and governance, privacy and data governance, robustness and safety, trust and human oversight, and regulatory compliance. Relevant studies were identified through Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, and supplementary Google Scholar citation tracking. The review applies a qualitative, theory-building narrative synthesis structured by sector and responsible-AI dimension. Strategic mechanisms are interpreted using resource-based and dynamic-capability perspectives. No statistical meta-analysis was undertaken. A total of 381 records were identified, 47 duplicates were removed, and 334 records underwent title and abstract screening. Following the exclusion of 191 records, 143 full-text articles were assessed. Seventy-nine full-text articles were excluded for documented reasons, resulting in 64 studies being included in the final synthesis. Two reviewers conducted screening independently, with disagreements resolved through discussion. Inter-reviewer agreement was substantial, with Cohen’s kappa of 0.80. This is a retrospective registration. The initial database searches were conducted between 12 and 27 February 2026, and update searches were conducted between 15 and 18 July 2026. Database searching, duplicate removal, screening, full-text assessment, data extraction, coding, and narrative synthesis were completed before this registration was created. The registration is being made in the interest of transparency and to support PRISMA 2020 reporting. No results-based changes were made to the research questions or eligibility criteria after screening commenced. The expected outputs include a systematic review manuscript, descriptive evidence tables, a cross-sector comparison of finance and healthcare, and an integrative model explaining how responsible-AI practices may develop into strategic organisational capabilities. The associated manuscript has been prepared for submission to the MDPI journal AI. The work was supported by Universiti Kuala Lumpur through the Center for Research and Innovation, and the authors declare no conflicts of interest.

documents.abstract: Purpose Job autonomy, intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction are typically treated as conceptually distinct constructs linked through causal or mediational relationships, yet survey-based studies consistently report strong empirical proximity among them even when they meet or approach conventional discriminant-validity standards. This conceptual paper asks what such structural relationships represent when conceptually distinct constructs are strongly intercorrelated in self-report models. Design/methodology/approach The paper develops an interpretive representation perspective treating self-reported motivation constructs as cognitively co-organized articulations of work experience. Survey data from 349 working adults serve an illustrative function, with each respondent providing ratings under two framings of their work experience (on-site and work-from-home) and partial least squares structural equation modeling examining within-person reweighting of structural configurations. Findings Autonomy, intrinsic motivation, and job satisfaction are generally psychometrically distinguishable yet structurally intertwined, with the closest construct pairings approaching conventional discriminant-validity thresholds. Differences across the two framings appear as selective reweighting of structural associations rather than uniform moderation or stable causal ordering, a pattern consistent with the interpretive representation account. Originality/value The paper offers a conceptual reinterpretation of a long-standing empirical regularity in organizational behavior research: strong covariance among motivation-related self-report measures is reframed as an expression of cognitive organization rather than evidence of causal sequencing. The argument complements established motivational theories and provides a more defensible basis for interpreting cross-sectional self-report SEM results, with implications for research practice and the use of employee survey data.

When an intuitive answer is uncertain, people are thought to engage in further reasoning. But what people actually do during this additional thinking, how it unfolds over time, and why it sometimes leads to better answers remain unclear. We scored think-aloud protocols with large language models to track, moment by moment, four possible functions of deliberation (generating candidate responses, justifying them, controlling intuitive responses, and regulating cognitive effort), together with expressed confidence. Deliberation showed a clear temporal organization: generation dominated early, whereas justification, control, and regulation became increasingly prominent as reasoning progressed. Correct responses involved more justification, control, and regulation than biased responses, and these evolving dynamics predicted accuracy for out-of-sample participants and items. Confidence and deliberation also showed reciprocal lagged associations: lower confidence predicted further generation, justification, and control, whereas regulation predicted subsequent increases in confidence. Deliberation, then, appears to involve not a single act of "thinking harder," but an evolving interplay of reasoning processes whose organization is linked to whether reasoning succeeds.

A systematic review was conducted to identify ergonomic risk factors associated with musculoskeletal disorders in the limbs of mining workers, the assessment methods used, and their relationships. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 53 studies from Scopus, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, MDPI, and IEEE Xplore (January 2015–May 2026) were included. Eleven risk factors were identified, with vibration (18 studies) and working hours (12 studies) being the most frequently reported. Five individual assessment methods (ISO/IEC 2631-1, REBA, OWAS, NIOSH, Risk Score), one symptom questionnaire (Nordic Questionnaire), and five hybrid/advanced methods (Bayesian Network + REBA, RULA + Nordic, SEM + Participatory Ergonomics, DMQ + Logistic Regression, RULA + Fuzzy Logic) were identified. Fifteen limb segments were evaluated, with the back (15 studies), shoulders (12 studies), and neck (12 studies) being the most studied, while wrists and elbows were notably absent. Hybrid methods demonstrated superior accuracy compared to individual approaches. Underground mining studies (58%) predominated over open-pit operations (42%). The findings provide an integrated framework connecting risk factors, affected limbs, and assessment tools. Critical gaps were identified, including the lack of wrist/elbow evaluation, underrepresentation of female miners, and absence of AI-based assessment systems. Four key challenges are proposed for future research, including developing deep learning-based ergonomic assessment tools and implementing real-time monitoring systems.

Undersea cables are essential to global digital connectivity and support cross-border energy transmission. They face accidental risks from anchoring, fishing and environmental hazards, alongside intentional disruption through espionage, sabotage and hybrid coercion. Governments, regional organisations and industry are developing frameworks to strengthen prevention, detection, response, repair and deterrence. The European Union's 2025 Action Plan illustrates a multidomain approach through regulatory enhancement, harmonised protection, real-time situational awareness and investment in repair capacity, including a cable-vessel reserve. Initiatives in the Indo-Pacific and Southeast Asia emphasise cooperative resilience-building and reduced regulatory barriers during emergency repairs, while industry guidance promotes governance, spatial planning and operational continuity. Nevertheless, protection remains fragmented because of jurisdictional gaps in exclusive economic zones and on the high seas, unequal monitoring and repair capabilities, and geopolitical competition over ownership, routing and standards. This study synthesises plans, identifies priorities and systemic gaps, and proposes strategies to enhance cable security and resilience.

Scientists across all disciplines share a common challenge: the divide between their theoretical knowledge and the specialized skills and time needed to build interactive tools to communicate this expertise. While large language models (LLMs) offer unparalleled acceleration in code generation, they frequently prioritize functional syntax over scientific accuracy, risking visually convincing but scientifically invalid results. This work advocates the Scientist-AI-Loop (SAIL), a framework designed to harness this speed without compromising rigor. By separating domain logic from code syntax, SAIL enables researchers to maintain strict oversight of scientific concepts and constraints while delegating code implementation to AI. We illustrate this approach through two open-source, browser-based astrophysics tools: an interactive gravitational lensing visualization and a large-scale structure formation sandbox, both publicly available. Our methodology condensed development to mere days while maintaining scientific integrity. We specifically address failure modes where AI-generated code neglects phenomenological boundaries or scientific validity. While cautioning that research-grade code requires stringent protocols, we demonstrate through two examples that SAIL provides an effective code generation workflow for outreach, teaching, professional presentations, and early-stage research prototyping. This framework contributes to a foundation for the further development of AI-assisted scientific software.

As Level 4 Robotaxis (RTs) transition into real-world deployment, understanding how passengers perceive driving behavior and form trust becomes increasingly critical. This study investigates the relationship between driving style, perceived aggressiveness, and trust across four urban driving scenarios using simulated RT videos. A total of 153 U.S. participants with prior RT experience evaluated simulated driving styles, their real-world counterparts, and their preferred styles. Results showed that perceived aggressiveness increased systematically with more aggressive driving styles and was significantly associated with decreased trust. Simulated driving styles at lower aggressiveness levels aligned closely with real-world perceptions, while higher levels deviated. Participants preferred more defensive driving styles than those perceived in real-world RTs. These findings suggest that passengers are sensitive to aggressive driving behaviors and may have lower tolerance in Level 4 contexts. The study provides insights for designing trust-aware driving strategies and highlights the importance of aligning system behavior with user expectations.

Optimizing astronaut mission readiness is a multidisciplinary endeavor that should integrate concepts from aerospace medicine, human performance, sports science, nutrition, and engineering. Situating astronauts within a theoretical framework similar to that of operational athletes, while addressing top human systems capability needs outlined for future missions, may be optimal for promoting sustained health and performance before, during, and after missions to low-Earth orbit, the lunar surface, and Mars. Mission readiness can be optimized by enhancing physiological and behavioral/psychological performance through data-driven and individualized exercise countermeasures, health and performance monitoring, precision nutrition, and rehabilitation strategies. Appropriate and stable space food systems that facilitate adequate provision of nutrients and fluids to prime astronauts for mission-critical tasks and operational demands are needed, though research is needed into potential nutritional considerations that might be useful for future missions. Behavioral readiness programs should emphasize stress inoculation, adaptive decision-making, communication, Earth-independent operation functionality, conflict resolution, leadership, and team-based problem-solving before flight to promote healthy team dynamics in-flight, along with proper society reintegration and uptake of family and occupational roles post-flight. Exercise remains an essential countermeasure during spaceflight, with an emphasis on maximizing fitness before launch to mitigate in-flight declines and on maintaining fitness levels and functionality during flight through high-intensity multimodal exercise. Following return to Earth, rehabilitative programs serve to restore cardiovascular, sensorimotor, and skeletal function, followed by enhancing skill-based performance components through a phase-based training program. Continuous monitoring systems that provide insight into health, performance, sleep, cognitive, nutritional, and recovery status should enable data-driven decision-making on physical readiness across all mission phases. By integrating insight from multiple disciplines, this unifying approach delivers a theoretical framework for sustaining astronaut health and performance during extended-duration missions.

Conventional flood cooling remains the dominant lubrication strategy in machining workshops worldwide, despite more than three decades of documented evidence concerning its environmental and occupational health costs. A single production facility may consume thousands of litres of cutting fluid annually, and the aerosol generated at the work zone carries well-documented associations with respiratory disease, dermatitis, and carcinogen exposure for operators. Over the same period, three categories of technical alternative have each developed substantial evidence bases: minimum quantity lubrication (MQL), nanofluid cutting fluids, and AI-driven process optimisation. No prior review has examined how these three strands fit together, or situated their integration within the Industry 5.0 framework, which holds that manufacturing must serve human well-being and ecological sustainability alongside productivity. This paper addresses that gap. Drawing on 125 primary publications from 2010 to 2025 identified through systematic database searches (methodology described in Section 1.1), the reviewed evidence indicates that nanofluid MQL can reduce cutting fluid consumption by 97 to 99.7 per cent relative to conventional flood cooling while achieving comparable or improved surface finish, tool wear, and cutting force outcomes across titanium alloys, nickel superalloys, stainless steels, and aluminium. This review assesses six nanoparticle classes in bio-based carrier fluids—including locally available West African oils that have received limited attention in the international literature—and examines AI and machine learning approaches for MQL optimisation with explicit attention to worker health outcomes. Eight research gaps are identified and a proposed three-horizon research agenda towards measurably low-impact machining practice by 2035 is presented.
